chapter.name: The Role of the Judiciary in Our Society

questions.q: Which line by Dr Martin Luther King Jr. opens the chapter on the judiciary?
questions.a: Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.
o: Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.
Where there is dharma, there is victory.
Every person is innocent till proved guilty.
Justice ensures that people can live with equality and dignity.

questions.q: The chapter opens with four Big Questions. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.a: How is a judge removed from office?
o: How is a judge removed from office?
What is the concept of justice?
What is the structure and role of the judiciary in India?
What are the alternative modes of dispute resolution?

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The judiciary plays a role in making sure that the executive does not overstep the role given to it by the Constitution.
Reason (R): The judiciary is a part of the executive, so it can supervise the executive from within.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The chapter says the judiciary keeps the executive within its constitutional role, but it is independent from the legislature and the executive, not a part of the executive.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Define the Judiciary as the chapter does, and give one example of a dispute it could settle.
questions.a: The Judiciary is the institution which ensures fair adjudication of disputes in accordance with the law and ensures that everyone is treated justly and with fairness. Example: a shop owner and a supplier who disagree over an unpaid bill can have their dispute decided by a court.
s: States that the Judiciary ensures fair adjudication of disputes in accordance with the law, treating everyone justly and fairly
Gives one suitable dispute between two parties, such as an unpaid bill between a shop owner and a supplier

questions.q: True or False? 'According to the chapter, as human societies grew larger and more complex, the task of ensuring fair treatment and peaceful living was given over to the government.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says societies expect fair treatment and peaceful living for everyone, and this task has now been given over to the government, which administers society through laws and ensures justice by framing laws.
s: Gives the verdict True
Gives the reason: governments were given the power to administer society through laws and to enforce them, and they ensure justice by framing laws

questions.q: A group of Class 8 students in Indore notices three things: (i) stray dogs in their colony are being poisoned; (ii) smoke from a factory is making people in a nearby settlement cough; (iii) two classmates have quarrelled over a borrowed cycle. The chapter says citizens have a role in helping the judicial system. (a) State that role as the chapter gives it. (b) Which of the three situations fit the kind of concern the chapter names, and whose rights does each affect? (c) Explain why situation (iii) is a different kind of matter.
questions.a: (a) Citizens help the judicial system by bringing to its notice social concerns that affect the rights of people, animals and nature. (b) Situation (i) affects the rights of animals and situation (ii) affects people (and nature, through the polluted air); both are social concerns of the kind the chapter names. (c) Situation (iii) is a private quarrel between two persons, not a social concern affecting the rights of many; it can be settled between them, for example by dialogue or mediation.
s: States the role: bringing to the judiciary's notice social concerns that affect the rights of people, animals and nature
Picks situations (i) and (ii), linking (i) to animals and (ii) to people or nature
Explains that (iii) is a private dispute between two persons, not a social concern, and can be settled between them

questions.q: Your class is making a five-panel wall chart titled 'The judiciary and justice'. Write one or two lines for each panel using the chapter: (a) the three kinds of justice the Preamble promises to all Indian citizens; (b) why justice is essential for any society; (c) the judiciary's place among the pillars of the government; (d) what the judiciary checks about the laws passed by the legislature; (e) what the judiciary checks about the executive.
questions.a: (a) The Preamble promises all Indian citizens social, economic and political justice. (b) Justice is essential for maintaining peace and harmony in a society, because it ensures that individuals can live with equality and dignity. (c) The judiciary is one of the three pillars of the government and is independent from the legislature and the executive. (d) It ensures that the laws passed by the legislature are within the framework of the Constitution. (e) It ensures that the executive does not overstep its role as outlined in the Constitution.
s: (a) Names social, economic and political justice
(b) Says justice maintains peace and harmony and lets individuals live with equality and dignity
(c) Places the judiciary as one of the three pillars, independent of the legislature and the executive
(d) States that it keeps laws passed by the legislature within the framework of the Constitution
(e) States that it keeps the executive from overstepping its constitutional role

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes a law, as the chapter defines it?
questions.a: A general rule made by the government to regulate activities, with consequences if not followed
o: A general rule made by the government to regulate activities, with consequences if not followed
A promise made in the Preamble that every citizen will always be treated with fairness and dignity
A decision given by a court in one single dispute between two named parties after hearing both
A settlement that two parties reach together with the help of a neutral mediator

questions.q: A school committee bars a Class 8 student from the sports meet for a whole year after a lab microscope is found broken. His parents make two complaints. Complaint 1: 'He was never allowed to explain that the microscope was already cracked.' Complaint 2: 'Even if he broke it, a whole year's ban is far too harsh.' Which aspect of justice does each complaint raise?
questions.a: Complaint 1: procedural justice; Complaint 2: substantive justice
o: Complaint 1: procedural justice; Complaint 2: substantive justice
Complaint 1: substantive justice; Complaint 2: procedural justice
Complaint 1: procedural justice; Complaint 2: procedural justice
Complaint 1: substantive justice; Complaint 2: substantive justice

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Criminal Tribes Act, 1871 has been repealed in independent India.
Reason (R): It labelled certain communities as criminals by birth, which was inconsistent with the values and principles of justice.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says such colonial laws were repealed because they were inconsistent with the values and principles of justice.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What has the government done, over the years, about the colonial-era laws that were found to be discriminatory? (b) Why were these laws found unfit for India after independence?
questions.a: (a) The government reviewed such laws and has repealed over 1500 of them, enacted during British rule. (b) They were discriminatory and contrary to the fundamental principles of a democratic polity, inconsistent with the values of justice and of India as a democratic republic.
s: (a) States that the government reviewed and repealed over 1500 laws enacted during British rule
(b) Gives the reason: they were discriminatory and contrary to the principles of a democratic polity and the values of justice

questions.q: (a) Name the three consequences the chapter lists for not following a law. (b) Which of the three does the chapter say applies only in some cases?
questions.a: (a) Paying a fine, giving compensation to the affected party, and imprisonment. (b) Imprisonment, which the chapter says applies in some cases.
s: (a) Names paying a fine, giving compensation to the affected party and imprisonment
(b) Identifies imprisonment as the one used only in some cases

questions.q: Answer briefly: (a) What does the chapter call the system that enables a person to complain in case of a grievance? (b) What does this system allow the affected person to do? (c) Within which two frameworks does it ensure justice?
questions.a: (a) The judicial system. (b) It allows the affected person to place their point of view. (c) Within the framework of the law and the Constitution.
s: (a) Names the judicial system
(b) States that the affected person can place their point of view
(c) Names the law and the Constitution

questions.q:
The residents' welfare association (RWA) of a building in Bhopal has a written rule: 'If water leaks from a flat into the flat below, the owner of the upper flat pays the repair bill.' In July, water from Mr Bose's bathroom leaked into Mrs Khan's flat, and her repair bill came to Rs 9,500. The RWA committee called both of them, heard each for half an hour and looked at photographs from both sides. It then ordered Mr Bose to pay Rs 9,500 for the repair and a further penalty of Rs 15,000, although no RWA rule mentions any penalty.
(a) Which aspect of justice is about every person getting a full opportunity of hearing before a decision is taken?
(b) Was that aspect met here? Give the fact from the passage that shows it.
(c) How much was Mr Bose ordered to pay in all, and how much of it had no rule behind it?
(d) Judge whether the committee's decision was just, using both aspects of justice.
questions.a: (a) Procedural justice. (b) Yes: the committee called both Mr Bose and Mrs Khan, heard each for half an hour and looked at photographs from both sides before deciding. (c) Rs 9,500 + Rs 15,000 = Rs 24,500 in all, of which the Rs 15,000 penalty had no rule behind it. (d) Only partly just. The procedure was fair, since both sides were heard. But substantive justice asks whether the outcome is fair, just and reasonable: the repair bill follows the written rule, while a Rs 15,000 penalty, more than one and a half times the damage and backed by no rule, is not reasonable. A just decision needs a fair hearing and a fair outcome, so the repair order can stand but the penalty should go.
s: (a) Names procedural justice
(b) Says yes, citing that both were heard and photographs from both were seen
(c) Finds Rs 24,500 in all and identifies the Rs 15,000 penalty as having no rule behind it
(d) Judges the decision procedurally fair but not substantively fair, because the penalty is unreasonable, and says what a just decision would keep or drop

questions.q: The students' parliament of a school in Pune is debating three draft rules. Rule 1: 'Students who live in the hostel may not use the main drinking-water cooler; a separate tap is kept for them.' Rule 2: 'Nothing may be printed in the school magazine that criticises the student council.' Rule 3: 'A student who damages a library book pays for a replacement copy.' Using the chapter, (a) which unjust law or laws described in the chapter does Rule 1 most resemble, and why? (b) Which unjust law described in the chapter does Rule 2 most resemble, and what freedom would Rule 2 take away? (c) Which of the chapter's named consequences of not following a law does Rule 3 impose, and is Rule 3 unjust in the same way as Rules 1 and 2? (d) Decide which rule or rules the parliament should reject, and give the chapter's reason why such laws were repealed.
questions.a: (a) The Jim Crow laws (the apartheid-era laws of South Africa are also accepted): they kept people of colour from using public facilities, such as water fountains, that were reserved for others; Rule 1 likewise keeps one group of students away from a shared facility. (b) The Vernacular Press Act, 1878, which restricted freedom of the press; Rule 2 would take away the magazine's freedom to print criticism. (c) Compensation to the affected party (paying for the damaged book). It is not unjust in the same way: it applies to anyone who damages a book, as a consequence of what the student did, and does not shut out or silence a group of people. (d) Reject Rules 1 and 2. The chapter says such laws were inconsistent with the values and principles of justice, and that restrictions of this kind prevented people from gaining access to public facilities and living a life with dignity.
s: (a) Names the Jim Crow laws (or the apartheid-era laws) and links Rule 1 to keeping a group from a shared public facility
(b) Names the Vernacular Press Act, 1878 and the loss of freedom of the press
(c) Identifies compensation and explains that Rule 3 applies to an act by anyone, not to a group, so it is not unjust like the others
(d) Rejects Rules 1 and 2 with the chapter's reason: inconsistent with justice, denying access to public facilities and a life with dignity

questions.q: On which date did the Supreme Court of India come into existence?
The chapter's simplified diagram of courts in India shows three levels. Which order runs correctly from the top level to the bottom level?
questions.a: Supreme Court, then High Courts, then District Courts
o: Supreme Court, then High Courts, then District Courts
High Courts, then Supreme Court, then District Courts
Supreme Court, then District Courts, then High Courts
District Courts, then High Courts, then Supreme Court

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Supreme Court of India.
I. Article 124 of the Constitution provides for its establishment.
II. It is seated in New Delhi.
III. A judge of the Supreme Court retires on reaching the age of 62 years.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. Statement III is wrong: a Supreme Court judge retires at 65 years.
o: I and II only
I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q: (a) What is the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court designated as? (b) Who appoints every judge of the Supreme Court, as per Article 124?
questions.a: (a) The Chief Justice of India. (b) The President of India.
s: (a) States the Chief Justice of India
(b) States the President of India

questions.q: True or False? 'A distinguished jurist can be appointed a judge of the Supreme Court only if he or she has also served as a judge of a High Court for five years.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. Besides being a citizen of India, a person needs to meet only ONE of three routes: a High Court judge for five years, OR an advocate of a High Court for ten years, OR a distinguished jurist in the opinion of the President of India. A distinguished jurist qualifies on that ground alone.
s: Gives the verdict False
Explains that the three routes are alternatives joined by 'or', so being a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion is enough by itself

questions.q: Answer in brief: (a) What does the chapter call the Supreme Court in relation to the Constitution of India? (b) What is the present strength of the Supreme Court, and how many persons does it make in all? (c) What does the Supreme Court's motto 'yato dharmastato jayah' mean, as the chapter translates it?
questions.a: (a) The final interpreter of the Constitution of India. (b) 33+1, that is, the Chief Justice of India and 33 judges, 34 persons in all. (c) 'Where there is dharma, there is victory.'
s: (a) States that it is the final interpreter of the Constitution
(b) Gives 33+1, the Chief Justice of India and 33 judges, 34 in all
(c) Gives 'Where there is dharma, there is victory'

questions.q: Two citizens of India are discussed for appointment as judges of the Supreme Court. Justice Nair has been a judge of the Kerala High Court for 3 years and, after that, a judge of the Madras High Court for 2 years. Mr Bose has been an advocate of the Calcutta High Court for 4 years and of the Patna High Court for 4 years, and has never been a judge. The President of India does not regard either of them as a distinguished jurist. A newspaper writes: 'Neither of them qualifies, because neither has served long enough in any one High Court.' (a) Which qualification route applies to each person, and how many years does each route require? (b) Work out each person's total years and say whether each meets the route. (c) Is the newspaper right? Give your verdict and say what reasoning it gets wrong.
questions.a: (a) Justice Nair: route (i), a Judge of a High Court (or High Courts) for five years. Mr Bose: route (ii), an Advocate of a High Court (or more than one High Court) for ten years. (b) Nair: 3 + 2 = 5 years, which meets the five years required. Bose: 4 + 4 = 8 years, which is 2 years short of ten, so he does not meet it. (c) The newspaper is wrong about Justice Nair: the chapter's words '(or High Courts)' let years in more than one High Court count together, so she qualifies. Its conclusion about Mr Bose is right, but for a different reason: he falls short because his total is only 8 years, not because his years were split between two High Courts.
s: (a) Matches Nair to route (i), five years, and Bose to route (ii), ten years
(b) Finds 3 + 2 = 5 (meets) and 4 + 4 = 8 (falls short of ten)
(c) Judges the newspaper wrong about Nair because years in more than one High Court count, and right about Bose only because his total is 8 years

questions.q: A Class 8 group is building a three-level model of India's courts (top, State level, District level) and has six cards to place. Card 1: 'Provided for by Article 124; seated in New Delhi.' Card 2: 'Article 214 says there shall be one in each State.' Card 3: 'Articles 233 to 237 regulate their organisation.' Card 4: 'Its judges retire at sixty-two.' Card 5: 'Judges of these courts at the District level are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court.' Card 6: 'Hears appeals from final orders of a High Court.' (a) Place Cards 1 and 6. (b) Place Cards 2 and 4. (c) Place Cards 3 and 5. (d) Name the three levels of courts in order from top to bottom. (e) Using any two cards, explain why the chapter calls the Indian judicial system a unified system rather than separate systems.
questions.a: (a) Cards 1 and 6 go at the top: the Supreme Court. (b) Cards 2 and 4 go at the State level: the High Courts. (c) Cards 3 and 5 go at the District level: the Subordinate Courts. (d) Supreme Court at the apex, High Courts at the State level, Subordinate Courts at the District level. (e) The levels are linked in one chain: the Supreme Court hears appeals from High Courts (Card 6), and the High Court is consulted when District Judges are appointed (Card 5) and supervises the subordinate courts, so the courts form one hierarchy, not three unconnected systems.
s: (a) Places Cards 1 and 6 with the Supreme Court
(b) Places Cards 2 and 4 with the High Courts
(c) Places Cards 3 and 5 with the Subordinate Courts
(d) Names the three levels in order: Supreme Court, High Courts, Subordinate (District) Courts
(e) Uses two cards to show the levels are linked in one hierarchy, which is why the system is unified

questions.q: A citizen wants to file a writ petition directly before the Supreme Court to enforce a Fundamental Right. Under which Article of the Constitution can she do so?
questions.a: Article 32
o: Article 32
Article 226
Article 124
Article 214

questions.q: In the first reported PIL, filed by the lawyer Mrs Kapila Hingorani, the Supreme Court ordered the release of under-trial prisoners in Bihar. What else did the Court do in that matter?
questions.a: It issued guidelines to release almost 40,000 under-trial prisoners throughout India
o: It issued guidelines to release almost 40,000 under-trial prisoners throughout India
It ordered the State of Bihar to build new jails for all of its under-trial prisoners at once
It referred the matter to the President of India for an advisory opinion
It sent the matter to the Patna High Court to be decided under Article 226

questions.q: (a) For what purpose has writ jurisdiction been given to the Constitutional Courts? (b) Name any two Fundamental Rights that the chapter lists as guaranteed to every citizen of India.
questions.a: (a) For the enforcement of the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution of India. (b) Any two of: Equality, Liberty, Right to Life, Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Religion.
s: (a) States enforcement of the Fundamental Rights in Part III of the Constitution
(b) Names any two rights from the chapter's list, such as Equality and Freedom of Speech

questions.q:
Match Column A with Column B.
Column A: 1. Article 32   2. Article 226   3. Article 21   4. Part III of the Constitution
Column B: P. The Right to Life, to which PIL gives meaning   Q. A writ petition directly before the Supreme Court   R. A writ petition before a High Court   S. The Fundamental Rights, such as Equality and Liberty
Choose the correct matching.

True or False? 'In the Vishaka case, the Supreme Court's guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace came more than fifteen years before the Government's Act on the subject.' Give the verdict and the reason with dates.
questions.a: True. The Supreme Court laid down the guidelines in 1997, and the Government enacted the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act in 2013, which is 2013 - 1997 = 16 years later.
s: Gives the verdict True
Gives 1997 for the guidelines and 2013 for the Act, a gap of 16 years

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A writ petition about a Fundamental Right violated only within the territorial limits of one State can be filed only before the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Reason (R): Writ jurisdiction has been conferred on the Constitutional Courts for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Writ jurisdiction does belong to the Constitutional Courts, but the chapter places a violation within one State before the High Court under Article 226; Article 32 is for issues with an all-India ramification.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q:
Lake Sagar (imaginary) lies wholly within one State and supplies drinking water to about 2 lakh people in three towns. A local newspaper reports that sewage and factory waste are being poured into it, and that cases of stomach illness in the three towns have risen from 600 to 1,200 in one year. No single family can afford a long court case, but Ms Joshi, a retired teacher, wants a court to act on behalf of everyone affected.
(a) Name the innovation of the Supreme Court that lets an issue of public concern like this reach a court.
(b) The illness figures show a threat to people's lives and health. Which right, under which Article, does the chapter say this innovation gives meaning to?
(c) Which PIL case named in the chapter took up environmental issues, and which two issues did it take up?
(d) Using the chapter's description of Articles 32 and 226, which court fits Ms Joshi's petition better, and why?
questions.a: (a) Public Interest Litigation (PIL). (b) The Right to Life under Article 21; illness cases doubled from 600 to 1,200. (c) M.C. Mehta v. Union of India, which took up the cleaning of the River Ganga and the protection of the Taj Mahal. (d) The High Court under Article 226: the chapter ties Article 226 to violations within the territorial limits of a State, while a petition under Article 32 before the Supreme Court is for an issue with an all-India ramification. This lake lies wholly within one State.
s: (a) Names Public Interest Litigation
(b) Names the Right to Life under Article 21
(c) Names M.C. Mehta v. Union of India with the River Ganga and the Taj Mahal
(d) Chooses the High Court under Article 226, reasoning from the lake lying within one State against the all-India test for Article 32

questions.q: The Centre and a State have a legal dispute. Under which Article does the Supreme Court have exclusive original jurisdiction to decide it?
questions.a: Article 131
o: Article 131
Article 136
Article 143
Article 141

questions.q: An industry in Kanpur loses a case before the National Green Tribunal. Its lawyer says: 'The Supreme Court hears appeals only from High Courts, so our only path is the Allahabad High Court.' Which correction does the chapter support?
questions.a: The Supreme Court also has jurisdiction to hear appeals from specialised tribunals like the NGT
o: The Supreme Court also has jurisdiction to hear appeals from specialised tribunals like the NGT
The Supreme Court can take up the matter only if the President refers it for an opinion
The NGT's orders are final and cannot be appealed against in any court at all
The matter must go straight to the Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction in Article 131

questions.q: Name the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court used in each case: (a) the President of India seeks the Court's opinion on a question of fact of public importance; (b) the Court hears a case against a High Court judgment in a criminal case involving a death sentence.
questions.a: (a) Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143). (b) Appellate jurisdiction (Articles 134 and 134A).
s: (a) Names advisory jurisdiction
(b) Names appellate jurisdiction

questions.q: State what each of these Articles provides about the Supreme Court: (a) Article 141; (b) Article 142; (c) Article 144.
questions.a: (a) The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India. (b) The Supreme Court has the power to pass any order that is necessary for doing complete justice. (c) All civil and judicial authorities shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.
s: (a) States that the law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts in India
(b) States the power to pass any order necessary for doing complete justice
(c) States that all civil and judicial authorities act in aid of the Supreme Court

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A dispute between two States over sharing river water is decided by the Supreme Court in its original jurisdiction.
Reason (R): The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within the territory of India.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Such a dispute goes to the Supreme Court because Article 131 gives it exclusive original jurisdiction over inter-state disputes; Article 141 is about the effect of its law on other courts.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A law student's notebook lists six Article numbers about the Supreme Court: 131, 132, 133, 134, 134A and 143. (a) Which Article gives the Court exclusive original jurisdiction, and between whom must the legal dispute arise? (b) Which Articles deal with appeals to the Court from High Courts? (c) Which Article covers the President of India's request for the Court's opinion, and at least how many judges must hear such a case? (d) A trader in Jaipur says: 'I will start my quarrel with a supplier directly in the Supreme Court under Article 131, because that Article lets the Court decide disputes from the start.' Use the chapter to explain why Article 131 does not fit his quarrel.
questions.a: (a) Article 131: legal disputes between the Centre and a State; between the Centre and a State on one side and another State on the other; and inter-state disputes such as river water disputes. (b) Articles 132, 133, 134 and 134A. (c) Article 143; such a case must be heard by a Constitution Bench of not less than five judges. (d) Article 131 covers only disputes in which the Centre and the States are the parties. A quarrel between a trader and a supplier is between private persons, not between the Centre and a State or between States, so it falls outside Article 131.
s: (a) Gives Article 131 with the Centre-State and inter-state disputes
(b) Groups Articles 132, 133, 134 and 134A as appeals from High Courts
(c) Gives Article 143 and a Constitution Bench of at least five judges
(d) Explains that Article 131 covers only disputes between the Centre and States or between States, so a private trader's quarrel does not fit

questions.q: Ramesh, a handloom weaver in Varanasi, supplied 400 sarees to a trader at Rs 1,250 each but was paid for only 250 of them. A lower court and then the High Court decided against him. His lawyer believes the courts misread their agreement. (a) How much money does Ramesh say is still due to him? Show the working. (b) Name the power of the Supreme Court, with its Article, that he can still ask for. (c) State the two grounds on which the chapter says the Court may grant it. (d) One ground uses the words 'substantive justice'. What does substantive justice focus on, as the chapter defines it? (e) Ramesh's cousin says, 'Your case is strong, so the Supreme Court is bound to hear it.' Is the cousin right? Justify from the way the chapter describes this jurisdiction.
questions.a: (a) 400 - 250 = 150 sarees unpaid; 150 x Rs 1,250 = Rs 1,87,500. (b) Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136. (c) Where a question of law of general public importance has arisen, or to do substantive justice between the parties. (d) Substantive justice focuses on the final result or outcome and asks whether the decision is actually fair, just and reasonable. (e) No. The chapter calls this an extraordinary discretionary jurisdiction: the Court may grant special leave, but it is not bound to; even a strong case is heard only if the Court decides to grant leave.
s: (a) Finds 150 unpaid sarees and Rs 1,87,500
(b) Names Special Leave to Appeal under Article 136
(c) Gives both grounds: a question of law of general public importance, or doing substantive justice
(d) Defines substantive justice as the fairness of the final outcome
(e) Judges the cousin wrong because the jurisdiction is discretionary, not a right

questions.q: Which Article of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court in each State?
questions.a: Article 214
o: Article 214
Article 124
Article 226
Article 233

questions.q: According to the chapter's table of High Courts, which High Court covers the State of Goa?
questions.a: Bombay High Court
o: Bombay High Court
Karnataka High Court
Kerala High Court
Gujarat High Court

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about High Courts.
I. Article 214 of the Constitution provides that there shall be a High Court in each State.
II. Every High Court has the same number of judges, whichever State it is in.
III. Each High Court exercises its powers within its territorial limits.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the chapter says the number of judges in a High Court varies from State to State.
o: I and III only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.q:
Match each Article in Column A with what it provides about High Courts in Column B.
Column A: 1. Article 214   2. Article 217(2)   3. Article 226   4. Article 227
Column B: P. The qualifications for appointment as a High Court judge   Q. A High Court in each State   R. The power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory   S. Writ jurisdiction of the High Court
Choose the correct matching.
(a) At what age do High Court judges retire? (b) Who appoints the judges of a High Court?
questions.a: (a) At the age of sixty-two years. (b) The President of India, in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State and the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court.
s: (a) States sixty-two years
(b) States the President of India (in consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the High Court's Chief Justice)

questions.q: Sunil says: 'Under Article 227, a High Court can step into the day-to-day work of every court and tribunal in its State whenever it likes, to run them better.' Test his claim using the chapter: (a) state the power that Article 227 gives a High Court; (b) state the nature and purpose of this power; (c) give your verdict on Sunil's claim.
questions.a: (a) Every High Court has the power of superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction. (b) The power is supervisory in nature; it is exercised to ensure that subordinate courts and tribunals act within the bounds of their authority and jurisdiction, and it is to be exercised sparingly. (c) Partly right: the High Court does have superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory, but it is a supervisory power used sparingly to keep them within their authority, not a power to run their daily work whenever it likes.
s: (a) States superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction
(b) States that the power is supervisory, keeps them within their authority and jurisdiction, and is used sparingly
(c) Gives the verdict partly right, with the reason

questions.q: Four students from different places want to know which High Court covers their home. Using the chapter's table of High Courts, name the High Court for each: (a) Kavya, who lives in Puducherry; (b) Tenzin, who lives in Arunachal Pradesh; (c) Mehak, who lives in Chandigarh; (d) Rafeeq, who lives in Lakshadweep.
questions.a: (a) Madras High Court. (b) Gauhati High Court. (c) Punjab & Haryana High Court. (d) Kerala High Court.
s: (a) Names the Madras High Court for Puducherry
(b) Names the Gauhati High Court for Arunachal Pradesh
(c) Names the Punjab & Haryana High Court for Chandigarh
(d) Names the Kerala High Court for Lakshadweep

questions.q: A Class 8 group sorts the 25 High Courts in the chapter's table into three groups. Group X: a High Court whose table entry names only one State or Union Territory. Group Y: a High Court that covers two or more States or Union Territories, at least one of them a State. Group Z: a High Court that covers two or more Union Territories and no State. (a) Which High Court belongs in Group Z, and what does it cover? (b) Name the High Courts that belong in Group Y, and give their number. (c) Using (a) and (b), work out how many High Courts belong in Group X. (d) How many of the Union Territories named in the table share a High Court with a State? Name them. (e) A student concludes: 'Every High Court in Group Y covers at least two States.' Use the table to decide whether she is right.
questions.a: (a) The Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court, which covers the Union Territory of Jammu & Kashmir and the Union Territory of Ladakh. (b) The Bombay, Calcutta, Gauhati, Kerala, Madras and Punjab & Haryana High Courts: 6 High Courts. (c) 25 - 6 - 1 = 18 High Courts. (d) 5: Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu (Bombay High Court), Andaman & Nicobar Islands (Calcutta High Court), Lakshadweep (Kerala High Court), Puducherry (Madras High Court) and Chandigarh (Punjab & Haryana High Court). (e) She is wrong. Only 3 of the 6 (Bombay, Gauhati, and Punjab & Haryana) cover two or more States. The Calcutta, Kerala and Madras High Courts each cover one State (West Bengal, Kerala, Tamil Nadu) together with one Union Territory.
s: (a) Names the Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh High Court with its two Union Territories
(b) Names the six Group Y High Courts
(d) Finds 5 Union Territories and names them
(e) Judges her wrong, using Calcutta, Kerala and Madras as High Courts with one State and one Union Territory

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT among the Subordinate Courts that the chapter lists?
questions.a: Lok Adalats
o: Lok Adalats
Sessions Courts
Revenue Courts
Small Causes Courts

questions.q:
Match each body in Column A with the disputes it decides in Column B, as shown in the chapter's figure on tribunals.
Column A: 1. Consumer Fora   2. National Green Tribunal   3. National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)   4. Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL)
Column B: P. Environmental issues   Q. Electricity disputes   R. Consumer disputes   S. Corporate civil commercial disputes, including insolvency and bankruptcy disputes
Choose the correct matching.

Assertion (A): The subordinate judiciary is a very important segment of the judicial system.
Reason (R): It is in the subordinate courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says the subordinate judiciary is very important because it is in these courts that the judiciary comes in close contact with the people.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter say a tribunal is, and under what are the specialised tribunals established? (b) A dispute related to the Armed Forces arises in an Army regiment, and a power company raises a dispute over electricity charges. Explain why the two disputes go to two different tribunals, naming each tribunal.
questions.a: (a) A tribunal is a committee or body established to settle certain types of disputes; the specialised tribunals are established under various enactments and are quasi-judicial in nature. (b) Each specialised tribunal decides only a specific category of disputes: the regiment's dispute is related to the Armed Forces, so it goes to the Armed Forces Tribunal, while the electricity dispute goes to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), which decides electricity disputes.
s: (a) Defines a tribunal as a body set up to settle certain types of disputes, established under various enactments
(b) Explains that each tribunal handles one category, naming the Armed Forces Tribunal and APTEL

questions.q: Answer briefly: (a) Name any two kinds of Subordinate Courts. (b) Which Articles of the Constitution regulate the organisation of these courts? (c) Who appoints the District Judges, and in consultation with whom?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: District Courts, Sessions Courts, Revenue Courts, Small Causes Courts. (b) Articles 233 to 237. (c) The Governor of the State, in consultation with the High Court (Article 233).
s: (a) Names two Subordinate Courts from the chapter's list
(b) States Articles 233 to 237
(c) States the Governor in consultation with the High Court

questions.q: Meera says: 'Tribunals are quasi-judicial bodies, so no High Court has any say over them, and the Supreme Court never hears appeals from them either.' Test both parts of her claim using the chapter, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Part 1 is wrong: a High Court entertains appeals against decisions of certain tribunals, and under Article 227 every High Court has superintendence over all courts and tribunals within its territorial jurisdiction. Part 2 is also wrong: the Supreme Court has jurisdiction to hear appeals from specialised tribunals like the National Green Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal. Verdict: the claim is wrong on both parts; tribunals are quasi-judicial, but they are not outside the control of the higher courts.
s: Shows part 1 is wrong: High Courts hear appeals from certain tribunals and have superintendence over tribunals under Article 227
Shows part 2 is wrong: the Supreme Court hears appeals from tribunals such as the NGT and NCLAT
Gives the verdict that the claim is wrong, while agreeing that tribunals are quasi-judicial

questions.q:
In Rampur village (imaginary), a stone-crushing unit has cut down 1,200 of the 5,000 trees in the community forest on which 3,500 villagers depend for firewood and grazing, and it plans to clear more. Separately, 40 families of the village each bought a water purifier for Rs 8,000 from a dealer who promised free servicing for two years; after six months the dealer stopped answering their calls. The sarpanch wants to take both problems to the right bodies, but the village can afford to pursue only one case this year.
(a) Which tribunal does the chapter name for environmental issues?
(b) Which body does the chapter name for the purifier buyers' complaint?
(c) How much did the 40 families pay for the purifiers in all?
(d) Which case should the village pursue first? Justify your choice using the chapter and the data.
questions.a: (a) The National Green Tribunal. (b) The Consumer Fora, which decide consumer disputes (the National Consumer Commission, named in the chapter's builder case, is also accepted). (c) 40 x Rs 8,000 = Rs 3,20,000. (d) The forest case first: it affects all 3,500 villagers, not only 40 families; nearly a quarter of the forest (1,200 of 5,000 trees) is already gone and more is planned, and felled trees cannot be put back quickly. The consumer complaint is about money, which a consumer body can order to be returned later, as in the chapter's builder case where the amount was returned with interest. (A choice of the consumer case is acceptable only if it is justified with both figures, for example that Rs 3,20,000 is a large loss for 40 families.)
s: (a) Names the National Green Tribunal
(b) Names the Consumer Fora (or the National Consumer Commission)
(c) Finds Rs 3,20,000
(d) Chooses a case and justifies it with both data points (3,500 villagers and the lost trees against Rs 3,20,000) and what each body can do

questions.q: Four people describe how their disputes were dealt with. Whose account agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: Asha's account: a Lok Adalat can resolve disputes that are pending in the courts, and it settles them amicably.
o: Asha: 'Our boundary case had been pending in the civil court for three years; we settled it amicably at a Lok Adalat instead.'
Bilal: 'The mediator heard both of us and then gave a decision that binds us and can be enforced by a court of law.'
Charu: 'Our arbitrator could not decide anything; she only helped us talk until we reached our own agreement.'
Dinesh: 'The Gram Nyayalaya could not hear us, because it sits only in the district town and follows the full formal procedure.'

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about digital technology in the judicial system.
I. Hybrid hearings and e-Filing are among the digital initiatives the chapter lists.
II. The 'Virtual Justice Clock' screen has stood at the main entrance gates of the Supreme Court since 1950.
III. Court judgments are translated into only two languages, English and Hindi.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. Statement II is wrong because the screen has been there since 2024-2025, and Statement III is wrong because judgments are translated into multiple Indian languages.
o: I only
I and II only
I and III only
II and III only

questions.q: Name the law of 2023 that has replaced (a) the Indian Penal Code, 1860, and (b) the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
questions.a: (a) The Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. (b) The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023.
s: (a) Names the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(b) Names the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023

questions.q: (a) State the two objectives with which Gram Nyayalayas were set up under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008. (b) Explain how their being mobile, village-level courts with a simplified procedure serves these objectives.
questions.a: (a) To decentralise the judicial system and to reduce the burden on regular courts. (b) Because they move to villages and decide disputes simply, without technicalities, villagers can get disputes settled near home instead of going to distant regular courts, which spreads the work out from the centre and leaves fewer cases for the regular courts.
s: (a) States decentralising the judicial system and reducing the burden on regular courts
(b) Links mobility and simple procedure to justice near home and fewer cases in regular courts

questions.q: True or False? 'In arbitration, the person who decides the dispute must always be a retired judge.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The chapter says an arbitrator can be a retired judge, a lawyer or an expert.
s: Gives the verdict False
Corrects it: an arbitrator can be a retired judge, a lawyer or an expert

questions.q: In an imaginary district, 2,400 cases are pending in the district court. On one day, a Lok Adalat settles 15% of these pending cases amicably. In the same month, a Gram Nyayalaya decides 180 village disputes that would otherwise have been filed in the district court. (a) How many pending cases does the Lok Adalat settle, and how many remain pending? (b) Which aim of Lok Adalats given in the chapter does this show? (c) Which objective of Gram Nyayalayas do the 180 disputes show, and why are they counted differently from the Lok Adalat's cases?
questions.a: (a) 15% of 2,400 = 360 cases settled; 2,400 - 360 = 2,040 remain pending. (b) Lok Adalats aim to reduce judicial backlog by settling disputes amicably, without the rigours of formal adjudication; they can resolve disputes already pending in the courts. (c) Reducing the burden on regular courts (and decentralising the judicial system). The 180 disputes were never filed in the district court, so they do not reduce the 2,040 pending cases; they stop new cases from being added.
s: (a) Finds 360 settled and 2,040 still pending
(b) States the Lok Adalat aim of reducing backlog through amicable settlement of pending cases
(c) Names the Gram Nyayalaya objective and explains that the 180 disputes prevent new filings rather than cutting the pending count

questions.q:
Savitri, a farmer in a village in Odisha, and her neighbour quarrel over who should pay for repairing the irrigation pump they share. The repair cost Rs 6,000. The nearest regular court is 70 km away. A mobile, village-level court set up under an Act of 2008 visits the village every month and follows a simplified procedure with no technicalities. Savitri's neighbour suggests that they could instead meet a neutral person who would only help them reach their own settlement.
(a) What is the mobile, village-level court in the passage called?
(b) What is the neutral person who only helps the parties reach a settlement called?
(c) If the two agree to share the repair cost equally, how much does each pay?
(d) Savitri wants a decision even if her neighbour does not agree. Which of the two routes should she choose? Give a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A Gram Nyayalaya. (b) A Mediator. (c) Rs 6,000 / 2 = Rs 3,000 each. (d) The Gram Nyayalaya, because it adjudicates on disputes, that is, it decides them; a mediator only assists the parties and has no power to make any decision or impose a view on them.
s: (a) Names the Gram Nyayalaya
(b) Names the Mediator
(c) Finds Rs 3,000 each
(d) Chooses the Gram Nyayalaya because it decides, while a mediator cannot impose a decision

questions.q: A district court in Odisha (imaginary) surveys 800 of its litigants. 45% say they cannot find out where their own case stands without visiting their lawyer. Another 160 say they cannot read the court's orders because copies are given only in English. The rest raise no complaint, and no litigant raises both complaints. The court can start only ONE digital project this year: Project P, a service that lets litigants check the details of their own cases directly; Project Q, free copies of its orders and judgments in Odia and other Indian languages; Project R, live streaming of its court proceedings. (a) How many litigants cannot find out where their case stands? Show the working. (b) How many litigants raise no complaint? (c) State the two qualities the chapter says digital technology has been introduced to give the judicial system. (d) Which project matches the chapter's second example of a use of digital technology, and what is that example? (e) Choose ONE project and justify your choice using the survey data and the chapter, saying why it serves this court better than the other two.
questions.a: (a) 45% of 800 = 360 litigants. (b) 800 - 360 - 160 = 280 litigants. (c) To make the judicial system more accessible and transparent. (d) Project Q: the chapter's second example is making copies of court orders and judgements freely available to the public, in multiple languages, so that anyone can read and understand the proceedings of the court. (e) Project P: it meets the larger need, 360 litigants against 160 for Project Q, and it is the chapter's own example of letting litigants check the details of their cases directly instead of only relying on their lawyers. Project Q would help only the 160, and Project R lets people watch hearings but answers neither complaint in the survey. (Project Q is acceptable only if the answer uses both figures and argues why the 160 need help more urgently.)
s: (a) Finds 45% of 800 = 360
(c) States accessible and transparent
(d) Names Project Q and the example of free court orders and judgements in multiple languages
(e) Chooses a project and justifies it with the data (360 against 160), comparing it with the other two
